sections.html:
• Name: Red claw crab (also Mini crab, Red crab, Grapsus bidens, Sesarma moeschi)
  • Scientific name: Perisesarma bidens, formerly Sesarma bidens
  • Minimum tank size: 45 litres
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Size: 10 cm across the leg span
  • Water type: slightly brackish (SG 1.005)
  • Optimal TDS: 150–200 (100–300)
  • Nitrate: less than 40 ppm
  • Diet: detritivore / omnivore
  • Temperament: aggressive
  • Life span: up to 2.5 years
  • Colour: shades of red to flaming orange with brown spots

Red claw crabs are one of the most traded crab species, and many retailers still sell them as "freshwater crabs" or "aquatic crabs". They are not fully aquatic: they can spend half of their time on land, which is crucial for their breathing.

They are not suited to a tank filled up with water. They need a piece of land, a log or a rock so they can reach the surface to breathe; otherwise they will drown.
This species is native to Asia, where it lives in shallow, warm coastal mangrove swamps.

Red claw crabs are classic brackish water mangrove crabs. Although they are often mistaken for freshwater crabs and can survive in freshwater, they do best in brackish water.

The shallow mangrove swamps where they are found often mix with seawater, which raises the salinity. This is where the misconception that they are freshwater crabs comes from. Mangrove swamps in general are freshwater rather than brackish, but those where red claw crabs live lie along the coastline, so the water always has some salinity.

Red claw crabs have a gill chamber (not a lung), located under the carapace near the first pair of walking legs. As long as their gills stay moist, they can be out of the water. Special plates keep the gills moist by shutting the opening in the exoskeleton so that dry air cannot get in. Although they have gills, they are semi-aquatic and also require fresh air.

They have two "teeth" (Latin bidens – having two blades or teeth) on the lateral sides of the carapace. The carapace of an adult only grows to about 3.5–5 cm long, with a leg span up to about 10 cm, so they are smaller than most aquarium crab species, which is why they are sometimes called Mini crabs.

Red claw crabs do best in a tank (paludarium) set up specifically for them, or an existing tank altered to meet their needs. Provide caves and rock crevices to hide in. A minimum of 45 litres is needed for one crab; it might do for two, provided they are not both male, as males will fight.

Despite their small size, they need a lot of space, and even a 45-litre tank can barely replicate anything close to their natural habitat. Some people keep them in 20-litre tanks, which is not recommended as it constantly stresses the crabs.

The water-to-land ratio should be at least 3 to 1. They spend almost 50% of their time on land. This is especially important with two crabs: because they are extremely territorial, if one claims a small bit of land, the other may not be "allowed" out at all.

Water changes should be done regularly. Remove leftover food that is more than 1–2 days old.

Molting: Because they have an exoskeleton, red claw crabs must molt to grow. The molt itself usually lasts only a few minutes, but the new shell then needs time to harden. The tank therefore needs plenty of hiding spaces, as the crab chooses one as a safe retreat while vulnerable, and may stay hidden for multiple days.

It takes weeks for a crab to prepare for molting. The day before, it stops eating and absorbs water, which makes the shell crack open around the body and the top lift up; the crab then removes itself from the old shell. Lost claws or legs regrow after two or more molts.

The cast-off exoskeleton resembles a fully intact, "dead" crab, so do not panic if you find one among the decorations. During hardening the crab is filled with water, extremely vulnerable and prone to injury. Do not remove the old exoskeleton: it contains a lot of calcium and the crab will eat it later.

Sometimes a molt fails and the crab cannot get out of its old shell. Once a molt goes bad, nothing can be done but wait and hope for the best.

Although they can survive in freshwater or saltwater, slightly brackish water with a pH of 7.2–8.5 is ideal. They prefer fairly hard water, as they come from Asian mangroves and estuaries.

A salinity tester, a good marine salt (Instant Ocean is suggested) and a thermometer/hydrometer are needed. Brackish water with an SG of 1.005 suits the species very well; this is a little less than a teaspoon of salt per 4 litres of water. Full seawater is 35 grams of salt per litre, so this is about 1/6 of normal seawater salinity.

When adding brackish water to the tank, mix it thoroughly in a bucket first. Never add salt directly to freshwater already housing the crabs, as the shock can hurt or kill them. Never use table salt in an aquarium.

They can live in freshwater, but it greatly decreases their lifespan, from 2.5 years in brackish water to a few months at most in freshwater.

Substrate: A sandy substrate (for example Carib Sea sand) is the best choice. The claim that gravel breaks off the tips of their legs is wrong; the real reason is that red claw crabs are burrowers, so they are better equipped for sand, which replicates their natural environment. They also strongly prefer natural refuges such as rock crevices, and spaces under and between boulders. Light-coloured sand gives a nice contrast with the crabs.

Land and perches: The crabs need perches above the water line, as they have to come to the surface to breathe. Driftwood and other perches made from natural materials are easy for them to use, for example a piece of driftwood sticking up out of the water. It is best if the crab also has a dry, mounted perch, floating on the water or mounted to the side of the tank, with a dry sandy substrate. Access to dry land is almost as important to their health as air. They prefer more humid conditions.

Lid: A tight-fitting lid is mandatory. Red claw crabs will escape if given the opportunity, so cover even the smallest gaps. Once outside the tank they die of dehydration within hours.

Heater: They come from a tropical region and need water temperatures that stay between 22 and 27°C at all times, with no drastic jumps between the high and low ends. If the room stays at that temperature even overnight, a heater is not needed; otherwise it is.

Lighting: There are no special requirements; it depends on the plants in the tank. Simple LED lighting that helps the plants grow is enough.

Filtration: Red claw crabs need a filter. The type depends first of all on the water level. These setups are most easily filtered with a canister or in-tank filter, and terrarium and paludarium filters for aquatic animals are available. Sponge and hang-on-back filters do not work well with lowered water levels.

In the wild, red claw crabs are scavenging omnivores. They eat almost anything, from algae and plant matter to small, slow-moving or weak fish and shrimp. They scavenge the bottom of the tank for scraps left by other animals and can be part of the cleanup crew.

Many prepared sinking foods, such as shrimp pellets, make a good main diet. Foods they will eat:

  • Shrimp pellets
  • Shrimp granules
  • Fish food (TetraMin flakes, etc.)
  • Shrimp food (Hikari Shrimp Cuisine, algae wafers, brine shrimp, etc.)
  • Frozen bloodworms
  • Vegetables such as spinach, peas, squash and leafy greens

Variety in food is always better, as the crabs get different necessary micronutrients. Like all invertebrates, they need calcium supplements in the water.

Red claw crabs are shy and nocturnal, and spend most of their time hiding. When they do explore, they usually scavenge along the bottom. They are excellent climbers and escape artists, moving quickly and walking with ease underwater.

They are territorial and very aggressive towards each other. When meeting a tank mate they often raise their claws defensively, which can quickly turn offensive, especially against a smaller tank mate. They are fairly skilled hunters when needed but prefer to scavenge. They make small dens under decorations and plants and retreat to them when threatened, and stay hidden there for several days while molting.

The level of aggression depends on the space and number of hiding spots, and even a 45-litre tank does not guarantee peace. Males fight for territory and dominance, as in the wild they have much more space. Females are less aggressive and usually just chase each other away. Red claw crabs are also very destructive and will "redecorate" the tank to their liking.

Males and females are easily distinguished. Males tend to be brighter and more colourful, and have a larger carapace (about 20 mm) than females (10–19 mm), so males are generally bigger. Males have larger, brighter claws and the underside of the shell is oblong or pointed. Females have smaller (about half the size), darker claws and a rounded (wider, oval) underside. The tips of the claws are yellowish, from pale to bright.

In the wild, red claw crabs mate only from April to September. Females can carry eggs again shortly after releasing their first batch of larvae, so each female can produce at least two broods a year. Mating rituals are unclear: males simply flip females over and pin them down. The smallest egg-bearing female recorded was 8.7 mm, so they reach sexual maturity at a relatively small size.

Incubation of fertilised eggs takes 20 days. The young begin life as larvae with no maternal care, and may become an easy meal for the adults. Under laboratory conditions complete metamorphosis takes from two weeks to more than a month (about 36 days), so it takes around 50–60 days from brood incubation for the young to become crabs.

Successful mating is rare in tanks and rearing the young is almost impossible, though not unheard of. There are 4 larval stages plus the megalopa stage (the final, semi-transformed stage). Each stage lasts 3–6 days and the megalopa about 5–9 days, depending on salinity and temperature.

Salinity is extremely important. In one experiment, larvae were exposed to eight salinities (0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35%). At 0 and 5% the larvae died within 12 hours without molting to the next stage. Optimal salinity was 20–30% for the first stage, 25–30% for the second and third stages, and 20–25% for the fourth and megalopa stages; overall, 25% is optimal for complete larval development.

In the experiment, newly hatched brine shrimp nauplii were fed every day. A separate rearing tank is needed for the larvae, with aerated water renewed 50% daily.

Plants: Red claw crabs and plants are not compatible. They eat, cut and uproot everything in the tank, so be ready for total destruction. Even regular feeding of lettuce, cucumber, zucchini or kale does not stop them eating plants. In an experiment, a small amount of Java moss, Java fern, Anubias, corkscrew Vallisneria, duckweed and Brazilian waterweed was added and the crabs ate everything.

Tankmates: These crabs are not social and tend to cannibalise in captivity. Males should never be kept together, as they fight over territory, often with deadly results; many aquarists report that males never get along, even with a lot of space. Multiple females can be kept with a single male.

Fast-swimming fish that stay in the upper levels, such as neon tetras, guppies and mollies, are suitable; the crabs will not bother them unless they are sick and weak. Their cutter-shaped claws are better for shredding leaf litter and picking up bits than catching prey, but there is always a risk of an occasional fish or shrimp being taken. They may hunt at night when fish sleep near the bottom, and will try to eat whatever hits the ground near them.

Do not keep them with:

  • Slower-moving, bottom-feeding fish, or fish big enough to eat them.
  • Freshwater fish: salinity and temperature requirements must be similar, and freshwater fish should never be put into brackish water.
  • Turtles, which will probably eat them eventually (depending on the turtle's size).
  • Dwarf frogs and snails, which the crab can injure and kill.
  • Dwarf shrimp: a healthy shrimp is hard for the crab to catch, but shrimp are an easy meal when molting.
  • Fiddler crabs: the fiddlers will usually lose the fight and weak ones are treated as live food.

Red claw crabs generally do best in a tank with nothing but themselves.
